name: Postman
tagline: API development and testing platform for developers.
description: Postman is an API workspace built on collections of requests, with environments, mock servers, JavaScript test scripts, and scheduled monitors.
pros: Requests, scripts, assertions, and environment variables live in one collection that teammates can fork and edit.
Mock servers let frontend work proceed against a stable response while the real endpoint is still being built.
Documentation renders from the collection itself, so published examples cannot quietly diverge from the requests being sent.
Monitors execute a collection against live endpoints on a schedule, turning request definitions into checks on production behavior.
Pre-request scripts and JavaScript assertions sit on the request itself, so signed headers and response checks repeat across a whole set.
cons: The free tier limits team collaboration and paid tiers are priced per user, so cost tracks the number of engineers in a workspace.
Collections are stored in Postman's own database or cloud workspace rather than as files, which puts API definitions outside repository review.
It is a client rather than a gateway: authentication, rate limiting, and versioning policy for the APIs themselves stay on the server side.

features.name: Request collections
features.description: Requests are grouped into reusable sets with parameterized variables, shared through workspaces and published to public collections.

features.name: Environment variable substitution
features.description: Selecting an environment swaps the values a request uses, so one collection targets local, staging, and production hosts.

features.name: Pre-request scripts
features.description: Scripts run before a request to compute values such as timestamps or signatures that the call depends on.

features.name: JavaScript response assertions
features.description: Checks on the response are written in JavaScript and stored alongside the request that produced the response.

features.name: Mock servers from collections
features.description: A collection can be served as a mock endpoint so client development continues before the real API exists.

features.name: Generated API documentation
features.description: Documentation is produced from the collection, keeping examples aligned with the requests actually defined.

features.name: Scheduled endpoint monitors
features.description: Collections can be executed against live endpoints on a schedule to watch production behavior without opening the client.

features.name: Public workspace sharing
features.description: Collections can be published for others to read, fork, and adapt, which is how popular APIs get reused rather than rebuilt.

content.title: Postman as an API workspace
content.body: Postman began as a request builder and now functions as a workspace around API work: collections hold requests, environments swap the values they use, scripts run before and after each call, and documentation, mocks, and monitors are derived from the same definitions. This repository records it at 4.6/5 from 1,180 reviews, ranks it first on its API management page, and describes it in the API tooling comparison here as the platform covering the full API lifecycle for teams that need design, testing, documentation, and monitoring in one tool.

content.title: Collections, environments, and variables
content.body: A collection is the unit of work. Requests are grouped into reusable sets, each parameterized so the same definition can point at local, staging, or production by selecting an environment, and variable substitution happens at send time — which is what keeps a large collection maintainable across three deployments of the same API. The comparison stored in this repository notes that collections live in Postman's own storage rather than in the project repository, a choice that makes sharing through a workspace easy and makes reviewing a collection through a pull request impossible without an export step.

content.title: Scripts that run around each request
content.body: Two extension points sit on every request. Pre-request scripts compute what the call needs — timestamps, signed headers, tokens fetched elsewhere — and test scripts assert on the response once it arrives, written in JavaScript and stored with the request. Because both live in the collection, a check defined for one endpoint can be reused across the set, and a failure surfaces as a test result rather than as something a person has to notice by eye. The API tooling comparison in this repository lists variable substitution, environment management, pre-request scripts, and JavaScript assertions as the core scripting surface.

content.title: Mock servers and rendered documentation
content.body: A mock server answers requests with recorded or scripted responses, which lets frontend work proceed against a stable contract while the backend is still moving; parallel frontend development is the reason mocks are named in this repository's tooling comparison. Generated documentation renders the same requests as a reference for whoever consumes the API, so published examples cannot drift away from what the team actually sends. Both features appear in that comparison among the reasons Postman is described as the broadest option in the category.

content.title: Monitors against live endpoints
content.body: Beyond design-time work, a collection can be executed on a schedule against an environment that is running. That turns a test suite written during development into a set of checks on production behavior, running whether or not anyone has the client open. Monitoring is named in this repository's API tooling comparison alongside documentation, mock servers, and workspaces as the capability that lifts Postman from request builder to lifecycle platform. Because a monitor executes the same collection, the definitions serve development and checking without being written twice.

content.title: How collections move between people
content.body: Postman's collaboration surface is where much of the product's design sits. Requests travel through an account rather than through files, which is why sharing, forking, and workspace membership are the mechanisms used to move a collection between people instead of attaching it to a pull request. The sharing paths recorded across this repository's notes are these:
items: Workspaces: collections are shared among members of an account, with the extent of that sharing shaped by the plan limits recorded in this repository's comparison.
Public collections: popular APIs are published as collections that teams fork and customize instead of rebuilding from scratch.
Forking: a copy lands in your workspace with its scripts and variables intact, ready to edit against your own endpoints.
Generated documentation: the rendered reference is what gets handed to whoever consumes the API.
Monitors: a scheduled run can be attached to a collection so endpoints keep being checked after the workspace is closed.

content.title: Seats, not request volume
content.body: Pricing on this page comes from the dataset: Postman is stored as Freemium with a list price band of $14-39/mo, and the API management ranking here repeats that band beside a 4.6/5 rating. The structural point from this repository's tooling comparison is that collaboration is what a plan gates — the free tier supports limited team sharing, and paid tiers add per-user cost as more engineers join. Budgeting therefore follows headcount in the workspace rather than request volume. Stored bands on this site are recorded figures, not quotes, so confirm current rates with the vendor.

content.title: Where Postman stops
content.body: Three boundaries are worth stating. Postman is a client and workspace, not an API gateway: authentication, rate limiting, versioning policy, and the servers themselves stay outside it. Collections are stored in Postman rather than in the project repository, so teams that want API definitions reviewed through pull requests need a file-based tool or an explicit export step. And per-user pricing means a workspace-wide rollout costs more than one team's seat count suggests, which the comparison in this repository flags as the limitation of its collaboration model.

content.title: Insomnia, Bruno, and OpenAPI tooling
content.body: The alternatives recorded in this repository's API tooling comparison are specific. Insomnia is the lighter client: quicker to open, smaller feature set, and without the built-in documentation, mocks, or monitoring. Bruno stores collections as plain files in the project repository, which brings version control and pull-request review but no cloud workspace and less mature scripting. Specification-first teams are advised there to build on OpenAPI and reach for Postman for ad-hoc requests. In the stored head-to-head files Postman at 4.6/5 sits above most neighbors and below GitHub at 4.7.

content.title: Where these judgments come from
content.body: This page was written from the vendor's own documentation, this repository's API tooling comparison, its ranking pages, and the stored head-to-head records; no requests were sent through Postman to produce it. The evidence describes a tool that fits teams wanting one place to build, test, document, and monitor HTTP APIs, and fits less well teams that require definitions to live as files in the repository or that need a gateway in front of their services. Stored rating: 4.6/5 from 1,180 reviews.

faqs.question: Where are Postman collections stored?
faqs.answer: In Postman's application database or cloud workspace rather than as files on disk — a distinction this repository's API tooling comparison draws when contrasting Postman with file-based clients.

faqs.question: What does the Postman free plan cover?
faqs.answer: This repository records limited team collaboration on the free tier, with paid tiers priced per user. The stored price band for Postman is $14-39/mo, recorded rather than quoted.

faqs.question: Can Postman replace an OpenAPI workflow?
faqs.answer: Not for specification-first teams. The comparison here recommends building on OpenAPI as the foundation and using Postman for ad-hoc requests, test runs, and monitoring.

faqs.question: How does Postman compare with Insomnia and Bruno?
faqs.answer: The same comparison places Insomnia as the lighter request builder and Bruno as the file-based client that lives in the repository, while Postman covers docs, mocks, and monitoring.

faqs.question: Where does Postman rank in this repository?
faqs.answer: First among four picks on the API management page, second among four on API testing behind GitHub, and fourth on the overall developer tools ranking stored here.

author: Marcus Rivera
learningCurve: Requests are immediate; scripting, environments, and monitor design reward practice over days rather than hours
whoShouldUse: Backend and frontend developers who design, test, document, and monitor HTTP APIs in one place, and teams that share collections across an account.
whoShouldNotUse: Organizations requiring API definitions to live as files under version control, and teams needing a gateway in front of their services for auth or rate limiting.
